narrative: Your predicted probability of leaving is 49.0%, meaning the model estimates roughly a one-in-two chance you will leave your job; under the promotion rule, that risk is high enough to deny the promotion, but it is a risk signal rather than a certainty. The model did not use your gender, age, or health issues. The strongest factor was your overall years of experience: at 1–5 years, the most common range among employees predicted to stay, it pushed toward staying. The second most important factor was that you report other job opportunities while working here; only about 23% of employees predicted to stay report the same, so this pushed toward leaving and is the clearest retention warning. The third factor was your view that you have received the promotion you deserved; this pushed toward staying, though less strongly than outside opportunities pushed toward leaving. Overall, the model sees meaningful leaving risk because outside opportunities were only partly offset by experience and current promotion satisfaction. Before a future promotion decision, you and your manager should discuss concrete career progression, whether outside opportunities are being actively considered, and what would improve stability and satisfaction. The organization should consider clearer promotion pathways, retention conversations, and reviewing job conditions so staying becomes the stronger signal.
